cet1.title: CET1 ratio & risk-weighted assets
cet1.content:
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is core equity capital (common shares, retained earnings, reserves, after regulatory deductions) divided by risk-weighted assets (RWA) — the regulator's primary measure of a bank's ability to absorb losses before it threatens depositors or needs a bailout.

For HSBC: management targets CET1 in a 14-14.5% band and returns capital above that via buybacks; RWA has been rising as the balance sheet grows even as legacy/non-core disposals free up capital under the Asia-pivot strategy.

What to watch:

  • CET1 falling toward or below the ~13% regulatory minimum plus buffers
  • RWA growing faster than earnings (capital-inefficient growth)
  • Buyback pace slowing when CET1 approaches the bottom of the target band

returns.title: ROE & ROTE
returns.content:
Return on equity (ROE) is annualised profit attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by average shareholders' equity. Return on tangible equity (ROTE) strips out goodwill and intangibles from the equity base, so it is the return banks and analysts actually target and compare across peers.

For HSBC: management's stated target is mid-teens ROTE; the gap versus ROE reflects goodwill largely from decades-old acquisitions (e.g. Republic New York, Household).

What to watch:

  • ROTE trending toward or away from the mid-teens target
  • ROTE swings driven by one-off items (impairments, disposal gains) versus underlying trading
  • Half-year figures are typically annualised — compare like with like

nimCostIncome.title: Net interest margin & cost-to-income ratio
nimCostIncome.content:
Net interest margin (NIM) is net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets — the spread the bank earns between what it pays depositors/wholesale funders and what it earns on loans and securities. Cost-to-income ratio is operating expenses divided by operating income — the bank-specific efficiency measure (there is no gross margin in a bank income statement).

For HSBC: NIM is sensitive to global rate cycles (HKD/USD rates especially, given the Hong Kong balance sheet); management is targeting cost-to-income into the low-to-mid 40s% as the simplification programme (Hang Seng privatisation, non-core disposals) removes duplicated cost.

What to watch:

  • NIM compression as rate cycles turn (falling rates squeeze deposit-funded banks)
  • Cost-to-income drifting up despite stated cost-out targets
  • H1 NIM is not directly comparable to FY NIM without checking the basis

navNta.title: NAV & NTA per share
navNta.content:
Net asset value (NAV) per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding — accounting book value per share. Net tangible asset (NTA) per share deducts goodwill and intangibles first, giving the tangible book value a bank could theoretically realise in a wind-down or that underpins a price-to-tangible-book valuation.

For HSBC: the market habitually values large banks on price-to-tangible-book (P/TNAV) rather than P/E; NTA growth plus dividends is a rough proxy for shareholder value creation between buyback and dividend decisions.

What to watch:

  • NTA per share growth versus ROTE — they should be consistent absent capital returns
  • Buybacks accretive to NTA per share only when done below book value

niiImpairment.title: Net interest income & credit impairment charge
niiImpairment.content:
Net interest income (NII) is interest earned on loans and securities less interest paid on deposits and wholesale funding — typically the largest single revenue line for a bank. Credit impairment charge (expected credit loss, ECL) is the expense taken for loans expected to turn bad; it is the bank equivalent of a bad-debt provision and moves inversely with the credit cycle.

For HSBC: NII is exposed to Hong Kong/mainland China commercial real estate and to global rate paths; impairment charges have been elevated on mainland China commercial real estate exposure through the current cycle.

What to watch:

  • Impairment charge spiking relative to NII — a sign of credit-cycle stress, not just growth
  • NII direction versus the rate cycle and loan growth

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For HSBC Holdings plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For HSBC Holdings plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For HSBC Holdings plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For HSBC Holdings plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
